correctness.summary: The finite-order upper bound follows from the cut-edge omission estimate used in the recent odd-degree k=2 theorem together with the sharp O-West bridge bound, and extends componentwise. Sharpness at every admissible order is proved by variable-order one-deficient Walecki blocks attached to a bridge-tree core; the block Hamilton cycles cover exactly all non-core vertices. A standalone construction verifier matched the stated degree, connectivity, bridge, and coverage properties on 565 parameter cases and checked the cubic specialization through order 498.

limitations: The theorem treats 2-regular subgraphs, not exact fixed-order k-regular coverage for k>=3.
The finite-order upper inequality and the cubic specialization are prior results and are explicitly credited.
Older factor-theory literature under different terminology and very recent parallel work remain residual originality risks.
Finite verification supports but does not replace the proof.
Independent audit has not been performed.

originality.scope: to the best of our knowledge
originality.summary: The 2026 Sivashankar preprint already contains the finite-order upper inequality in the proof of its sharp asymptotic odd-degree k=2 result and gives equality constructions on the arithmetic progression (r^2-3)t+2(r+2); these are not claimed new. The cubic fixed-order function is also known from Choi-Kim-Kostochka-Park-West. Searches of the recent 2-factor literature and equivalent fixed-order/cut-edge formulations found no general odd-degree construction filling every admissible order. The originality claim is the all-orders interpolation and resulting exact fixed-order function; older differently phrased factor literature and very recent parallel work remain residual risks.

review_statement: Same-model review: passed. Independent audit: not yet performed.

value.summary: The result converts a sharp asymptotic theorem and sparse endpoint examples into a closed exact extremal function at every admissible order, with connected extremizers and an explicit order cost for each forced omitted vertex.
